title: Crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:11–21)
hook: Paul confronts Peter over eating apart from Gentiles; I live, yet not I
tomorrow: Paul lists three pairs. why does the third one break the pattern?

segments.voice: Yesterday Paul told his own story: a persecutor stopped in his tracks, and the line, by the grace of God. Today that same Paul walks into a room where people are eating.
screen: `BY THE GRACE OF GOD.` → `A ROOM WHERE PEOPLE ARE EATING.`

segments.voice: Nobody announces a seating chart. Somebody just picks up a tray and moves, and everybody sees it. Antioch. A shared table. Peter, the apostle, has been eating with Gentile believers, people who aren't Jewish, bread passed hand to hand. Then visitors arrive from James in Jerusalem. And Peter picks up his plate. Galatians says "he withdrew and separated himself." Other Jewish believers follow him. Even Barnabas, Paul's own partner on the road, goes with them. Paul is across the room, watching. He doesn't wait for a quiet word later.
screen: `A SHARED TABLE IN ANTIOCH.` → `PETER PICKS UP HIS PLATE.` → `PAUL IS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: "I withstood him to the face." Paul says it happened "before them all." Two Jewish believers in Jesus, Peter and Paul, arguing in public about who eats with whom. For Paul, a split table says something false about the good news, and he explains why. A person, he says, is put right with God by faith in Christ. Christians read that line in more than one way, and Jewish readers understand the law on their own terms; this is an argument among believers in Jesus, about their own table. Then Paul stops arguing and talks about himself: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me." The old Paul, the man who once sorted people into insiders and enemies, has died with Christ. What's alive in him now is Christ. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: Paul's most personal sentence about his inner life sits in the middle of a fight about lunch. That's the point. If Christ lives in Paul, and in the Gentile across the room, how can they eat apart? And Peter's answer? The letter never tells us.
screen: `I WITHSTOOD HIM TO THE FACE.` · `PUT RIGHT BY FAITH IN CHRIST.` · `YET NOT I, BUT CHRIST LIVETH IN ME.` · `HOW DID PETER ANSWER?` · then, large: `CHRIST LIVES IN ME.`

segments.voice: Choose one table in your week: lunch at work, a family dinner, a group chat that works like a table. Name who usually ends up at the other one, what keeps you apart, maybe only habit, and one small step you could take, a pulled-out chair or a plain "sit with us." If you pray, you can hold that person's name before God while you breathe.
Crucified with Christ. Paul's words for an old self that died with Christ, so that Christ now lives in him.
Your line: Christ lives in me, said in the middle of an argument about lunch. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Galatians 2:20 is a verse some Christians learn by heart, and some congregations keep shared meals meant to cross lines of background, from fellowship suppers to the Lord's table.

fork.setup: your team eats at two tables, starters and bench, mixed lately. when the coaches walk in, a senior starter you look up to moves to the starters' table. what's the Antioch move?
options: follow the senior; it keeps things smooth with the coaches.
stay at the mixed table, and say plainly why the split matters.
stay quiet now, and text the senior about it next week.
fork.reveal: Peter moved when the visitors came, and Paul withstood him to the face, before them all. if Christ lives in both tables, a split says something false.

original.note: Greek: I have been crucified with; one word in Galatians 2:20.

trapdoor: what you thought: crucified with Christ is a picture of harsh self-punishment.
what it means: Paul says his old self died with Christ and Christ now lives in him, which is why a divided table troubled him.
what a scholar hears: the Greek is one compound word, synestauromai, 'co-crucified', in a tense for something done that still holds.
guess: Paul's old self died with Christ, and Christ lives in him
Paul's vow to be put to death on a cross like Jesus
a ritual in which believers act out the crucifixion
recall: God loves one who gives gladly

chat.says: the spanish church that meets in our building at 2 shares our kitchen. we've never once eaten together. weird?
options: Kind of. Paul called Peter out over a split table: if Christ lives in both, why eat apart?
Not really. Separate tables keep the peace; Peter moved his plate to avoid a big fight.
Only if they've asked. Paul's point was to wait until the other group invites you over.
chat.meaning: In Antioch Peter withdrew from the Gentile believers' table, and Paul withstood him: if Christ lives in each of them, a split table says something false.

Antioch.meaning: a city where Jewish and Gentile believers ate together

Barnabas.meaning: Paul's partner on the road, who also left the table

James.meaning: a leader of the believers in Jerusalem
